scenario: You notice a small crack in the sidewalk and spend twenty minutes imagining what kind of object caused it, worrying it could injure someone.
A coworker sends a short email without the usual pleasantries, and you spend the afternoon replaying every previous interaction to find proof you offended them.
You are at a dinner party, and someone mentions a hobby you haven't kept up with in years, making you feel intensely embarrassed as if your life has been a failure.
A minor scratch on your car appears while you are looking for a parking spot, and you spend the rest of the day unable to focus on anything else.
A friend sends a late-night meme, but you are too anxious to respond immediately, fearing the wrong reaction will ruin your standing in the group.
You hear a strange noise coming from the upstairs apartment while you are alone, and spent the next forty-eight hours quietly planning an escape route and buying locks.
You see someone coughing in the grocery aisle, and you become convinced they have a contagious disease, changing your grocery list based on that fear.
You trip and stumble at a crowded street crossing, and you stare at the ground for three minutes to ensure no one saw you.
An old acquaintance sends a generic holiday greeting, and you immediately start analyzing the wording to see if they are trying to reconnect or if it is a mistake.
You try to make a sandwich and get the ingredients slightly wrong, and you spend the morning deliberating over what went wrong and why you cannot be careful.
A coworker is slightly late to a meeting, and you begin a silent internal investigation into why they came late and whether it signals a deeper commitment issue.
You are watching a movie and feel a sudden unease at the end, looping the last ten minutes five times to check if you missed a threatening detail.
A new coworker asks about your weekend and you over-analyze the timing and body language you mistakenly see as judgmental rather than curious.
You get a small splinter while gardening and spend the hour worrying it has become infected, despite no visible signs of inflammation.
A friend shares a mundane story about a trivial inconvenience, and you feel a wave of inadequacy thinking other people have it much better than you.
You are waiting for a text from someone you like and you flip back and forth between messages nervously like a monkey.
A knock at the door comes just after you made a secret comment, and you turn every part of your conversation over to interpret the timing as a hidden signal.
You notice a change in the budget spreadsheet and spend three hours checking every department, each entry, and each category for an error.
You see someone putting on makeup in a public restroom and feel confident in your own ability to manage your body and the immediate world without alteration.
You are at a restaurant and wait a minute for your order, and you spend the next ten minutes anxious about why the delay happened and what it means for your evening.
A phone call drops a split second before the end, causing you to replay the missed words so often you cannot sleep that night.
You receive a notification about a price increase on a subscription and immediately start budgeting and cutting costs before the increase actually happens.
You are walking home at dusk and the streetlights flicker, making you scan every shadow for a threat to your safety.
You attempt a mental exercise with a dissociative patient and are able to fully immerse yourself in the patient's perspective to understand their state of mind.
A partner makes a joke that is clearly meant to be playful, and you react with a somber silence because you are too focused on the potential for hurt.
You are filling out a form from an old binder and become fixated on the blackness of the ink and the ink coming from the pen.
You are shopping for household cleaning supplies and experience a sharp, sudden loss of interest as you realize nothing needs cleaning.
You are planning a weekend trip and calmly pick out guides for the route, the hotel, and the meals while surrounded by books and newspapers.
You notice a dusty corner in your backyard and feel a sudden urge to clean the entire house, sweeping away everything before you turn on a light.
You have a conversation with a colleague and immediately question every pause the other person made for what they might have intended to convey.
You watch your own reflection in a store window and hope it is a new stranger, not you.
A coworker sends an email with minor grammatical errors, and you spend fifteen minutes mentally constructing a polite but firm response about professionalism.
You are waiting for a bus and feel your hands shaking because you are worrying about what happens a day from tomorrow.
You go to a job interview and hear a question and immediately worry about the disaster of the future.
You receive a compliment about your work and immediately think about the one thing that wasn't included in the praise.
Your alarm clock fails to go off on time, and you are flooded with images of everything that would be ruined.
While at work, you cannot focus on your primary task because you are thinking about a trivial little detail that matters nowhere but your current immediate life.
You are at a store and a clerk confuses a copy number for a customer number, and you feel your blood pressure rise.
You have a date with a partner and, you know something is wrong. You can feel it.
You receive an invitation to a party and immediately spend the hour worrying about what you will wear, who will be there, and whether anyone will notice.
You are driving and see a cyclist in the street and panic about what could happen next.
A friend calls and asks how you are doing, and you feel overwhelmingly guilty about every time you answered the phone before or after the scheduled moment.
You are walking down a street and step on a piece of glass and immediately worry about a cut, then a wound, then an infection.
You check your bank account balance every ten minutes, even though you know you haven't made a purchase since last night.
You are at a party and cannot pick a pin to choose what to wear to the next event you have to attend.
You are working on a project and cannot write down the plan in advance, but you know you can do the work just by starting it.
You are looking for a key you lost in the morning, and three hours later you find it in your coat pocket, which seems entirely irrational and absurd.
You organized your bookshelf and decided on an order that seemed perfect for you, but you changed it again that night because it didn't feel right.
You receive an email with a subject line that made you pause in shock, even though your brain went over it and you knew it was unrelated to you.
You are sitting at a bus stop and watching the people coming and going, and you feel an overwhelming sense of anxiety over being seen.
